_readme: Which optional data bundles are actually shipped, and why any of them is not. This file is COMMITTED and always present; the app reads it before reaching for a bundle, so a deliberately-absent file is answered from data rather than from a 404. That matters twice: the console stays clean (acceptance criterion 1 is 'no console errors', and a 404 is a console error even when it is expected), and BITE can print a sentence somebody wrote on purpose instead of an HTTP status. Each entry carries a SHORT reason, which is what an instrument flag shows, and a longer detail, which is what the BITE page adds underneath it. scripts/build-navdata.mjs rewrites the navdata entry when it emits the bundle.

navdata.detail: Run `npm run navdata` with the OurAirports CSVs. The session that built this app could not fetch them: the egress proxy denies davidmegginson.github.io, and Doctrine §15 says report that rather than route around it. No panel in v1 reads navdata, so nothing on screen depends on it.

geoid.reason: no geoid model bundled — GPS altitude is shown as GEOMETRIC, uncorrected
geoid.detail: Without a geoid model, GPS height above the WGS84 ellipsoid cannot be converted to altitude above mean sea level, so indicated altitude, pressure altitude, TAS and CAS all read FAIL and the tape is labelled GPS ALT. Typing approximate separation values would make every one of those look right and be wrong by tens of feet — the exact defect v1 exists to forbid. The expected file shape is documented at the top of src/data/geoid.js.

wmm.reason: no World Magnetic Model coefficients bundled — declination unavailable
wmm.detail: True/magnetic conversion is therefore unavailable. The evaluation algorithm is implemented and tested in src/data/wmm.js; it needs NOAA's published WMM.COF wrapped as {"cof": "<file text>"}. The coefficients are 90 numbers, and approximating them from memory would produce a plausible, wrong declination on a value a pilot uses to reconcile a compass against a GPS track.
